textbookText: Histologically, each testis contains hundreds of microscopic convoluted tubular units called the semeniferous tubules. The wall of semeniferous tubule is lined by germinal epithelial cells or primordial germ cells which later transform into sperms by the process of spermatogenesis. The space between the semeniferous tubules is filled with the connective tissue, blood capillaries, nerve fibers and interstitial cells. The interstitial cells secrete a male sex hormone called testosterone, which produces the secondary sexual characters in breeding season such as development of vocal sacs, nuptial pads etc. The sperms are arranged in the form of sperm bundles and nourished by nurse cells. A mature sperm is elongated microscopic cell with three distinct parts: head, middle piece and tail. A conical cytoplasmic structure present on top of the head is called acrosome which is used for the penetration of the egg membrane during fertilization as it contains a chemical called sperm lysine. In the middle piece, mitochondria and two centrioles are present. Tail helps in movement of sperm. Some yellowish finger like outgrowths are found attached nearer to the anterior region of each testis which are fat-bodies, used up at the time of hibernation.

b) Vasa efferentia: There are 10-12 very fine tubes emerging from the testis to the kidney. The vasa efferentia traverse through the mesorchium and open into Bidder’s canal along the inner margin of each kidney. The sperms from the lumen of semeniferous tubules are passed into Bidder’s canal via vasa efferentia and then carried to longitudinal collecting tubule through the transverse collecting tubules. Longitudinal tubule leads posteriorly into urinogenital duct. c) Urinogenital duct: Each kidney gives rise to a white muscular tube called urinogenital duct or ureter at its outer border which transports both sperms and urine. Each urinogenital duct runs posteriorly and opens into the cloacal chamber. In some frog, it dilates to form a seminal vesicle to store the sperms temporarily. Seminal vesicles are not found in Rana tigrina. d) Cloacal chamber and Cloacal aperture: It is a common chamber that receives faecal matter, urine and sperms. All these products are discharged out through cloacal aperture. Copulatory organ is absent in frog. After amplexus or pseudo copulation, the male frog sheds sperms on the female’s ova.

Ovaries: They are paired, irregular shaped, blackish white, lobulated structures, each attached to the dorsal wall of abdomen, and kidney with the help of thin membrane known as mesovarium. Ovaries become enlarged during breeding season and female’s belly become bulging. The ovaries have no internal connections with the kidneys. During the breeding season, the wall of the ovarian follicles ruptures to release the ova into the coelom which is called ovulation.

Histologically, ovary is a thin walled sac that contains many lobules. Each lobule consists of outer layer of theca externa and inner layer of theca interna with connective tissue in between. Connective tissue contains blood vessels, nerves etc. Theca externa is internally lined by germinal epithelial cells at certain places which undergo oogenesis to form ovum. The ovum is surrounded by single layer of follicular cells, which in turn enveloped by the extension of theca interna. Each unfertilized ovum is blackish white large cell and is surrounded by vitelline or egg membrane. Upper pole of ovum is called animal pole and lower pole is called vegetal pole. Ovum is furthermore surrounded by albumin which protects the egg from desiccation and external infections. Egg of frog is mesolecithal i.e. containing moderate amount of yolk and telolecithal i.e. yolk concentrated towards vegetal pole.
